design_detail: Between-subjects vignette experiment, called randomized by the authors, in which two versions of a questionnaire were handed out alternately to attendees present at the start of two addiction-focused talks at two mental health/addiction-focused conferences in October 2008 (location not stated). The two vignettes are identical except for the term: Mr. Williams, attending a court-ordered treatment program that requires abstinence from alcohol and other drugs, had two positive urine drug screens and a positive breathalyzer reading a month earlier and a further positive urine screen since, and now awaits the judge; he is described either as 'a substance abuser' or as having 'a substance use disorder' (the term appears twice in each version). Participants rated their agreement (1 to 6) with 32 statements; three subscales were derived by exploratory factor analysis of the pooled answers and compared between versions with independent t-tests at a significance level of .025 per comparison. 728 people were handed a form and 516 completed it (71%). No behaviour or real decision was measured.
can_establish: That among these conference attendees, described as mental health care providers (64.5% with doctoral-level degrees), reading the version that called the man 'a substance abuser' went with slightly more agreement with a mixed set of culpability, punishment and non-medical statements than reading the version that said he had 'a substance use disorder' (subscale means 2.92 vs 2.82 on a 1–6 scale), with no detectable difference in willingness for social contact or in treatment-related items.
cannot_establish: Whether the term changes what clinicians actually do, the care patients receive or their help-seeking; whether the effect holds for other scenarios (one vignette only, a man under court supervision with positive drug tests), other professionals, the public or policy makers; whether the difference is reliably above zero (the printed p of .02 matches an unstated one-sided test, allocation was by alternation and 29% did not take part); or that the terms leave social-contact and treatment judgments unchanged (differences of about d 0.2 were not excluded).

sample.recruitment: Conference attendees present at the start of two addiction-focused talks at two mental health/addiction-focused conferences in October 2008, each with a single stream of presentations; the location of the conferences is not stated; participants were not compensated (Method › Study population and protocol, 1st paragraph, p. 203; Measures, 2nd paragraph, p. 204).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No eligibility or exclusion criteria: all attendees who chose to complete and return the questionnaire (Method › Study population and protocol, 3rd paragraph, p. 204).
sample.demographics: 516 completers: mean age 51; 63.4% women; 81.0% White; 64.5% with a doctoral-level degree; professional focus (more than one allowed) mood disorders 66.9%, anxiety disorders 59.9%, psychosis 37%, alcohol/drug problems 34.8% (Results, 1st paragraph, p. 205). Professions (psychologist, psychiatrist, social worker and so on) are not reported, nor are characteristics by version.
sample.attrition: 212 of the 728 people handed a form (29%) did not complete it; the authors say they do not know why (Limitations, p. 206). Completion by version is not reported. The perpetrator-punishment test has 504 degrees of freedom, implying 506 analysed, so 10 completers are missing from it without explanation (Results, 3rd paragraph, p. 205).
sample.selection_effects: Attendees of addiction-focused talks at mental health conferences: mostly doctoral-level and White, with a mean age of 51 and only about a third reporting an alcohol or drug focus. The forms, with the term already in the vignette, were handed out before people decided whether to take part, so taking part could follow reading the term; 29% did not take part, for unknown reasons and in unknown proportions by version. The authors themselves caution against generalizing to mental health providers or other groups (Limitations, p. 206).

exposure.measurement: Version of the questionnaire received. The two forms were handed out alternately and sequentially by study staff through the auditoria; the authors describe this as an even and random distribution that removed seating biases (Method › Study population and protocol, 2nd paragraph, p. 204). No other randomization procedure is described.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable. Each version used its term twice in an otherwise identical paragraph (Fig. 1, p. 203); completing the questionnaire took about 20 minutes (p. 204).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable. The vignette's character was required to abstain from alcohol and other drugs and had positive urine drug screens (drug not named) and a positive breathalyzer reading (Fig. 1, p. 203).

comparison.controls: Attendees who received the version saying that Mr. Williams has (and has had for the past few years) 'a substance use disorder'.
comparison.matching: Allocation by alternation of the two forms. The authors report that the versions did not differ on any measured variable (chi-square and t-tests, ps > .17), but give neither the group sizes nor the characteristics by version (Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph, p. 204).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Participants' prior attitudes towards people who use drugs, their profession, addiction training and personal or family experience of substance use were not measured, or are not reported by version.

outcomes.instruments: 32 statements rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 6 (strongly agree). By the source column of Table 1, 21 come from the 1996 General Social Survey mental-health module (Pescosolido et al., 1996), 3 from Kloss and Lisman (2003) and 8 from the authors (editors' count; the text says eight were written by the authors and the majority came from the General Social Survey, Measures, 1st paragraph, p. 204). Exploratory factor analysis of all 516 (principal axis factoring, oblique Promax rotation, loading threshold .32) gave three factors explaining 33% of the variance: 'perpetrator-punishment' (14 items, α .80), 'social threat' (4 items, α .86) and 'victim-treatment' (8 items, α .64); one cross-loading item was dropped and five further items loaded on no factor (editors' count from Table 1) (Results, 2nd paragraph, p. 205; Table 1, p. 204).
outcomes.validity_norms: The subscales were derived from this sample's own answers and have no external validation; the authors call for their reliability and validity to be confirmed in other samples (Limitations, p. 206). Content (Table 1, p. 204): 'perpetrator-punishment' mixes punishment by the judge (disciplinary action, 200 hours of community service, a jail sentence as a wake-up call, harsher consequences for further use), causes (poor choices, a reckless lifestyle, the way he was raised, God's will), responsibility and avoidability, violence to himself or to others, and referral to a religious leader or a spiritual or natural healer; 'social threat' consists only of willingness to have him as an employee, close friend, neighbour or co-worker; 'victim-treatment' mixes referral to treatment, self-help, family and medication with genetic and chemical-imbalance causes and expected severity. The scoring of the subscales (direction; mean or sum) is not stated; the printed means of 2.82 and 2.92 imply item means on the 1–6 scale, below its midpoint of 3.5.
outcomes.operationalization: Stigma was operationalized as agreement with the 14-item 'perpetrator-punishment' subscale (culpability and punitive or non-medical responses), with willingness for social contact ('social threat') and with endorsement of treatment and biological causes ('victim-treatment'). No behaviour, real decision or patient outcome was measured.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Significance level set at .025 per comparison for the three t-tests, citing Benjamini and Hochberg (1995, 2000) (Statistical analysis, 4th paragraph, p. 205). How .025 follows from that procedure is not explained: applied to three tests at a false discovery rate of .05, it would require the smallest p-value to be at most about .017 (editors' calculation).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Self-completed questionnaire. Each participant read only one version; what participants were told about the purpose of the study is not reported. The staff handing out the forms knew the alternation.

analysis.effect_sizes: 'Perpetrator-punishment': 'substance abuser' version mean 2.92 (SD 0.57) vs 'substance use disorder' version 2.82 (SD 0.58); t = 2.05, 504 df, p = .02; d = 0.20 as printed, called small by the authors (Results, 3rd paragraph, p. 205). Editors' calculations: for t = 2.05 with 504 df the two-sided p is about .041 and the one-sided p about .020, so the printed p matches a one-sided test; d from the printed means and SDs is about 0.17 (0.16 to 0.19 allowing for rounding of the means) and from t and df about 0.18, with an approximate 95% CI of 0.01 to 0.36 assuming two groups of about 253; the mean difference of 0.10 scale points has an approximate 95% CI of 0.00 to 0.20. 'Social threat' and 'victim-treatment': no significant differences (ps > .59), with no means, SDs or test statistics printed. Editors' calculation: with about 253 per group, p > .59 implies |d| below about 0.05, with 95% intervals reaching up to about ±0.22. Subscale intercorrelations: 'social threat' with 'perpetrator-punishment' Spearman r = −.27 (p < .01), described as more willingness for contact going with less agreement with disciplinary measures; 'victim-treatment' unrelated to both (p > .05) (Results, 2nd paragraph, p. 205).
analysis.covariates: None (unadjusted independent-samples t-tests); demographic balance checked with chi-square and t-tests (p. 204).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, registration or pre-specified analysis plan is mentioned. The study was approved by the Partners Healthcare Human Research Committee; consent was given by continuing past the consent page (Measures, 2nd paragraph, p. 204).
analysis.selective_reporting: Group sizes are not reported. Means and test statistics are printed only for the subscale that differed. The hypothesis that the 'substance abuser' term would raise perceived ability to self-regulate (Introduction, 6th paragraph, p. 203) was not tested as its own outcome: of the three self-regulation items from Kloss and Lisman, two entered the 'perpetrator-punishment' subscale and one ('capable of overcoming his problem on his own') was dropped for cross-loading (Table 1, p. 204; Results, 2nd paragraph, p. 205). Item-level differences between versions are not reported. That p = .02 is one-sided is not stated.
analysis.power: Not reported. Editors' calculation: with about 253 per group the study had about 50% power to detect d = 0.2 at a two-sided α of .025 (about 61% one-sided).

interpretation_gap.results_show: One of three factor-derived subscales differed: readers of the 'substance abuser' version agreed slightly more with a mixed set of culpability, punishment and non-medical statements (2.92 vs 2.82 on a 1–6 scale, both below the scale midpoint; d about 0.2). Its printed significance (p = .02) corresponds to an unstated one-sided test; two-sided, p is about .04 (editors' calculation), above the authors' own .025 threshold. No difference was detected in willingness for social contact or in treatment-related items, but differences of about d 0.2 were not excluded.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that even among highly trained mental health professionals the two terms evoke "systematically different judgments" and that the 'substance abuser' term may perpetuate stigmatizing attitudes (abstract, p. 202). The Conclusions suggest that national institutes, health care organizations, policy makers and criminal justice systems may wish to reconsider their terms, and argue that less perceived stigma would lead people to seek help sooner (p. 206): help-seeking was not measured. The Limitations suggest the difference might be larger among legislators or policy makers, which was not tested (p. 206). The title and abstract call the study randomized, while the Methods describe forms handed out alternately (p. 204). Against this, the Limitations state plainly that the effect was small and that its translation into real-world decisions or actions is unknown (pp. 205–206), and the Conclusions add an argument that does not depend on the effect's size: the 'abuser' label gives no gain in descriptive precision, so dropping it should do no harm (p. 206).

timeline.event: Kelly's proposal for more precise addiction terminology ('Toward an addiction-ary'), cited as a source of this study's hypothesis (Introduction, p. 203); not read.

This study: 516 conference attendees; a small difference on a culpability-and-punishment subscale between the 'substance abuser' and 'substance use disorder' versions of one vignette, none on social contact or treatment items.

Kelly, Dow & Westerhoff (2010, Journal of Drug Issues), a companion experiment on whether the choice of substance-related terms influences perceived need for treatment, named on the project's reading lists as not found in PubMed; not read.

Pennington et al.: pre-registered online vignette experiment on other labels ('chronically relapsing brain disease' vs 'problem'; drug use vs a health concern) in a non-clinical sample, not on these two terms (card sc_pennington_2023).

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no direct replication of the 'substance abuser' versus 'substance use disorder' contrast appears in the sources read for this card. The project's language-and-stigma list names later word-choice experiments (Ashford, Brown & Curtis, 2018; Goddu et al., 2018) that are not yet appraised; the one appraised later experiment (Pennington et al., 2023) tested other labels in a non-clinical online sample. The study remains a single, small effect in one clinician sample and one scenario.

funding.funder: Massachusetts General Hospital Institutional Grant #020753 (title-page footnote, p. 202).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors: Center for Addiction Medicine, Department of Psychiatry, Massachusetts General Hospital (Harvard Medical School), Boston. The hypothesis draws partly on the first author's earlier proposal for more precise terminology (Kelly, 2004, cited p. 203). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered experiment with computer-generated, concealed allocation and full reporting of group sizes and all outcomes, testing person-first terms against labels across several vignettes (not only a court-supervised relapse) in clinicians and in the public, with decision outcomes (for example sanction and treatment recommendations), two-sided tests and equivalence bounds; and, beyond vignettes, studies of whether the terms used in records or by services change the care actually given or people's help-seeking.

domains.note: Forms were handed out alternately and sequentially (p. 204): the sequence was not random and was known to the staff handing them out, and people held a form, with its term, before deciding whether to take part. The authors report no differences on measured characteristics (ps > .17) but give no group sizes or values. RoB 2 treats allocation by alternation as not concealed.
Each participant read one version and was analysed by the version received; with alternation, neighbouring attendees probably held different versions, and whether any compared them is not reported.

29% of those handed a form did not complete it and 10 completers are missing from the main test; numbers and reasons by version are unknown (pp. 204–206), and willingness to complete an attitude questionnaire may depend on the attitudes it measures.

Self-reported agreement immediately after the vignette. Participants knew the term they had read, and in an audience attending addiction talks the term may have cued socially desirable answers, which the authors suggest may have operated (p. 206). The subscales were built from these data without external validation; 'victim-treatment' α .64.

No protocol or analysis plan; the outcome scales were derived after data collection (from the pooled answers, without reference to version); the printed p = .02 matches an unstated one-sided test; the other two subscales are reported only as ps > .59; the self-regulation hypothesis was not analysed as stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Allocation by alternation and 29% non-participation with an unknown split by version each give high risk under RoB 2, and the result itself is fragile: a difference of 0.10 on a 1–6 scale (d about 0.2) whose printed significance relies on an unstated one-sided test at a threshold that the cited procedure does not yield. The study may be cited for a small difference, in this sample of conference attendees, in agreement with culpability and punishment statements after reading 'substance abuser' rather than 'substance use disorder' in one court-supervision vignette, and for no detectable difference in willingness for social contact or in treatment items. It may not be cited as showing that the term changes clinicians' decisions, patients' care or help-seeking, as showing a large or systematic effect, or as showing that the terms make no difference to social distance.

key_findings.finding: 728 conference attendees were handed one of two questionnaire versions, alternately and sequentially; 516 completed it (71%), taking about 20 minutes; there were no eligibility criteria and no compensation.
key_findings.locator: Method › Study population and protocol, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Measures, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The two vignettes differ only in the term: Mr. Williams 'is a substance abuser' and 'has been a substance abuser for the past few years', or 'has a substance use disorder' and 'has had a substance use disorder for the past few years'. In both he attends court-ordered treatment requiring abstinence from alcohol and other drugs, had two positive urine drug screens and a positive breathalyzer reading a month ago and another positive urine screen since, and awaits the judge.
Completers: mean age 51; 63.4% women; 81.0% White; 64.5% with a doctoral-level degree; professional focus mood disorders 66.9%, anxiety disorders 59.9%, psychosis 37%, alcohol/drug problems 34.8%.

Factor analysis of the questionnaire items gave three factors explaining 33% of the variance, with a loading threshold of .32: a fourteen-item 'perpetrator-punishment' subscale (α .80), a four-item 'social threat' subscale (α .86) and an eight-item 'victim-treatment' subscale (α .64); the item 'capable of overcoming his problem on his own' was dropped for loading similarly on factors 1 and 3. 'Social threat' and 'perpetrator-punishment' correlated negatively (r = −.27, p < .01); 'victim-treatment' was unrelated to both (p > .05).
key_findings.note: Editors' count from Table 1: 32 items in all; 14 + 4 + 8 enter the subscales, one was dropped for cross-loading and five load at least .32 on no factor.

key_findings.finding: On 'perpetrator-punishment', readers of the 'substance abuser' version scored 2.92 (SD 0.57) and readers of the 'substance use disorder' version 2.82 (SD 0.58): t = 2.05, 504 df, p = .02, d = 0.20, described by the authors as a small effect.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: the two-sided p for t = 2.05 with 504 df is about .041; the printed .02 is the one-sided value, and no one-sided test is stated. d recomputed from the printed means and SDs is about 0.17, and from t and df about 0.18.

key_findings.finding: No significant differences between versions on 'social threat' or 'victim-treatment' (ps > .59); no means, SDs or test statistics are given for these subscales.

The 'social threat' subscale consists of four willingness items (as an employee, close friend, neighbour, co-worker; loadings .686 to .848). The two violence items load on 'perpetrator-punishment' (.350 to himself, .434 to others), as do upbringing as a cause (.444), God's will (.378) and referral to a religious leader (.498) or a spiritual or natural healer (.484).

The items the authors report as most strongly associated with 'perpetrator-punishment' are a reckless lifestyle as cause (.69), being responsible for causing the problem (.59), a jail sentence as a wake-up call (.53) and poor choices as cause (.51).

The versions did not differ on any measured demographic variable (ps > .17); the significance level for the three subscale t-tests was set at .025 per comparison, citing Benjamini and Hochberg (1995, 2000).

The authors' limitations: the difference was significant but small; whether differences of any size on these scales translate into real-world decisions or actions is unknown; the 71% response rate was less than ideal and the reasons for non-participation are unknown, so generalization should be cautious; the subscales need confirmation in other samples.

The authors conclude that it may matter how people with substance-related conditions are described, propose 'substance use disorder' or 'substance-related problem or condition' instead of the 'abuser' label, and suggest that institutions, policy makers and criminal justice systems reconsider their terms.

reporting_issues.issue: The only significant result is printed as t = 2.05, 504 df, p = .02, and the paper does not say that a one-sided test was used. By the editors' calculation, for these values the two-sided p is about .041 and the one-sided p about .020.
reporting_issues.consequence: Under a two-sided test the difference would not meet the authors' own threshold of .025 per comparison; the evidence for any difference is weaker than the paper presents. The directional hypothesis (p. 203) could justify a one-sided test only if planned, which cannot be checked without a protocol.

reporting_issues.issue: The threshold of .025 per comparison is attributed to Benjamini and Hochberg (1995, 2000), and how .025 was obtained is not explained. By the editors' calculation, that step-up procedure with three tests at a false discovery rate of .05 would require the smallest p-value to be at most about .017.
reporting_issues.consequence: Even the one-sided p of .02 would not pass the cited procedure as usually applied; the claim of significance rests on an unexplained threshold.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of participants in each version is never reported, and the perpetrator-punishment test has 504 df where 516 completed the questionnaire. By the editors' arithmetic, 504 df implies 506 analysed, so 10 completers are missing from the test without explanation.
reporting_issues.consequence: Balance between versions, differential non-completion and the precision of the estimates cannot be checked; the editors' intervals assume two groups of about 253.

reporting_issues.issue: The printed d of 0.20 is larger than the d implied by the printed means, SDs, t and df. By the editors' calculation, d is about 0.17 from the means and SDs and about 0.18 from t and df.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the effect is small on any of these figures, as the authors say; claims should give it as about 0.2 or less.

reporting_issues.issue: The title and abstract call the study randomized; the Methods describe forms handed out alternately and sequentially, with no random sequence described.
reporting_issues.consequence: The allocation was quasi-random (alternation); the study should be described as an experiment with alternating allocation, and its risk of bias rated accordingly.

reporting_issues.issue: The subscale labels do not match their content: 'social threat' contains only willingness for social contact (no threat or violence item), while the two violence items, an external cause (the way he was raised), God's will and religious or spiritual referral load on 'perpetrator-punishment', which the authors interpret as internal causal attribution and culpability.
reporting_issues.consequence: The null result on 'social threat' concerns social distance, not perceived dangerousness; the positive result is a difference on a heterogeneous 14-item composite of punitive, moral and non-medical statements, not specifically on internal attribution.
